summary: Defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that hand a client a list of IP addresses and domain names for IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services servers (see RFC 5677). A mobile device can learn where to find those servers when it joins a network.

eli5.summary: When you walk into a new building, the front desk gives you a list of helpers and where to find them. These new DHCP options are that list, handed to a device when it joins a network.

questions: how to find mobility service servers with dhcp
how does a mobile node find an 802.21 server
subtitle: DHCP options that tell a mobile device which servers offer IEEE 802.21 handover help.

tldr.problem: A mobile node needs to find servers providing IEEE 802.21 Mobility Services (information, event and command) when it joins a network, and a server may host only some of these services.
tldr.mechanism: Four new options, two for DHCPv4 and two for DHCPv6, carry either a list of IP addresses or a list of domain names, with sub-options that select the service type: IS, CS or ES.
tldr.outcome: A mobile node asks for the option in its request list and the DHCP server answers with the matching servers. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 5678 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2009, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It remains the specification of these DHCP options.

sections.title: Finding Mobility Services
sections.content:
IEEE 802.21 defines three service types to help link layer handovers across different technologies, called Media Independent Handover (MIH) services: Information Services (IS), Event Services (ES) and Command Services (CS). A mobile node (MN) may use any of them separately or together, and a Mobility Server may not host all three, so the MN needs to discover each service type separately.

RFC 5678 defines new DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options and sub-options, the MoS IP Address and Domain Name List Options, that let the MN locate a Mobility Server hosting the service type it wants. Apart from manual configuration, this is one of the possible ways to find such a server. The framework is in RFC 5677.
sections.eli5: Some helpers give you maps, some warn you about changes, and some tell you what to do. This document is a way for a device to ask which helper is where.

sections.title: The Option Formats
sections.content:
Each option starts with an option code and a length, followed by one or more sub-options. The length does not count the option code or itself. When a DHCPv4 option would exceed 254 octets, the procedure of RFC 3396 MUST be used to split it.

There are two kinds of option per protocol version. The MoS Address Option carries IP addresses and the MoS Domain Name List Option carries fully qualified domain names (FQDNs). In DHCPv4 the code and length are 1 octet each. In DHCPv6 they are 2 octets each, and so are the sub-option code and length.

Each sub-option begins with a sub-option code and a length. Address lists are in order of preference, which the client processes in decreasing order. If no server is available the length is 0, and otherwise it is a multiple of 4 for IPv4 or 16 for IPv6.
sections.eli5: Each option is a labelled envelope. The label says what is inside and how big it is, and inside are smaller envelopes for each kind of helper.

sections.title: Option Codes and Service Types
sections.content:
The four options and their codes are OPTION-IPv4_Address-MoS (139), OPTION-IPv4_FQDN-MoS (140), OPTION-IPv6_Address-MoS (54) and OPTION-IPv6_FQDN-MoS (55).

The sub-option codes pick the service: 1 for IS, 2 for CS and 3 for ES. They are the same in all four options.

Domain names use the label encoding of RFC 3315 Section 8. A sub-option MAY hold several names, but they should refer to the NAPTR records of different providers, not to different A records within one provider. The client MUST try them in the listed order, using the mechanism of RFC 5679, and resolves later names only if the first failed or shared no transport protocol with the server.
sections.eli5: Number 1 means maps, 2 means commands and 3 means events. If the card lists several offices, you try the first, and only go to the next if the first does not work.

sections.title: How Clients and Servers Use Them
sections.content:
The mobile node may discover a Mobility Server when it first joins a network or when it needs the service. It may also do so if it lacks network information, or wants to change servers, for instance to recover from a single point of failure.

In DHCPv4 the client MUST include a MoS Address Option or a MoS Domain Name List Option in the Parameter Request List. In DHCPv6 it MUST include one in the Option Request Option. The client MAY name the services it wants using sub-option codes, but SHOULD be ready to receive other sub-options or not get the ones it asked for.

A server that receives such a request MUST include the option in its reply. It MAY restrict the reply to the requested sub-options. If it finds no Mobility Server for a requested sub-option, it SHOULD return that sub-option with its length set to 0.
sections.eli5: The device says "please tell me about the helpers". The server writes the list, and if there is no helper of some type, it writes that type with an empty list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 2131 apply. If an attacker changes or inserts a DHCP response, the mobile node could be led to a rogue Mobility Server that supplies wrong information, events or commands for handover.

The RFC recommends DHCP authentication (RFC 3118) where available, which also helps against denial-of-service attacks on DHCP servers. Where it is not available, lower-layer security may be enough. For name resolution it recommends considering DNSSEC (RFC 4033).
sections.eli5: If someone slips a fake card into your hand, you could end up asking the wrong helper for advice. Checking that the card really came from the front desk prevents that.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigns option codes 139 and 140 for DHCPv4 and 54 and 55 for DHCPv6. The document also creates two registries for the sub-option field: "IEEE 802.21 Service Type" for DHCPv4 and "IEEE 802.21 IPv6 Service Type" for DHCPv6.

Values 1 to 3 are allocated to IS, CS and ES. The values 0 and 255 are reserved in the DHCPv4 registry, and 0 and 65535 in the DHCPv6 one. New values need Standards Action.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official list of labels, so everyone uses the same numbers for the same things.
